extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate or beginning graduate students in analysis/harmonic analysis
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of the Schwartz space, Fourier transform on RN, Poisson summation/integral formulae, and the Hilbert transform — including definitions, key propositions, constructions (bump functions), and boundary/convergence properties. Suitable for students learning techniques used in PDE, signal processing, and harmonic analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Schwartz function / Schwartz space S(RN)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Schwartz function on RN is a smooth function such that P(x) Q(D) f is bounded for each pair of polynomials P and Q. The Schwartz space S(RN) is the set of all Schwartz functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: e^{-π|x|^2} is Schwartz since its iterated derivatives are polynomials times e^{-π|x|^2}. The space S is a vector space closed under differentiation and multiplication by polynomials; elements are rapidly decaying and all polynomially-weighted derivatives are bounded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic functional inclusions and integrability of Schwartz functions
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is Schwartz then for every pair of polynomials P and Q, P(x)Q(D) f is bounded and in fact integrable: (1+|x|^2)^N P(x)Q(D) f is bounded for suitable N, hence f ∈ L1 ∩ L2 ∩ L∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these integrability properties when applying Fourier transform and convolution operations; S is a convenient subspace on which the Fourier transform and differentiation interact nicely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fourier transform preserves Schwartz space; inversion holds on S
rubrics_metrics.description: The Fourier transform F is one-to-one from S(RN) onto S(RN), and the Fourier inversion formula holds on S(RN).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposition 8.10: use the concrete formula for the Fourier transform on Schwartz functions and the Riesz–Fischer / Plancherel machinery to show F(S)=S and that inversion and norm-preservation properties apply within S.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction/existence of compactly supported smooth bump functions (C∞_comp)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given K compact and U open with K ⊆ U, there exists ϕ ∈ C∞_comp(U) taking values in [0,1] and identically 1 on K (Proposition 8.12). Lemma 8.11 constructs radial bump functions used in this proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The construction uses smooth one-dimensional cutoff functions and dilations; these bump functions show that C∞_comp(U) is nontrivial and can be extended by zero outside U. They are used to produce many Schwartz functions (via Fourier transform).

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation-invariant bounded operators on L2 are multipliers (Multiplier theorem)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is a bounded linear operator on L2(RN) that commutes with translations, then there exists an L∞ function M (the multiplier) such that A f = F^{-1}( M · F f ) for all f ∈ L2. M is unique a.e. and ||M||∞ = ||A|| (Theorem 8.14).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lemma 8.13: such A commute with convolution by any L1 function. The proof builds approximating Schwartz/L1 functions to define M locally in L2 and then patch to an L∞ function. Use density of C∞_comp in L2 and Plancherel to deduce existence and uniqueness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commutation with convolution by L1 functions
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is bounded on L2 and commutes with translations, then A commutes with convolution by any L1 function (Lemma 8.13).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This fact is used to move between operator action and multiplication on the Fourier side; proof uses approximation of L1 functions by finite linear combinations of translates and boundedness of A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poisson Summation Formula for Schwartz functions
rubrics_metrics.description: If f ∈ S(R1) then for all x, sum_{n∈Z} f(x+n) = sum_{n∈Z} Ff(n) e^{2π i n x} (Theorem 8.15).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: form the periodic function F(x)=∑_n f(x+n), compute its Fourier series (period 1), interchange sums/integrals using uniform convergence on bounded intervals; applies directly to Schwartz functions where all required convergence is uniform. Remark: generalizes to locally compact abelian groups with discrete subgroup and compact quotient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gaussian identity / application of Poisson Summation
rubrics_metrics.description: Corollary: For any r>0, ∑_{n∈Z} e^{-π r n^2} = r^{-1/2} ∑_{n∈Z} e^{-π n^2/r} (Corollary 8.16).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Poisson Summation to appropriate Gaussian dilates; this identity underlies the functional equation for the Riemann zeta function after further analytic continuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poisson kernel for the upper half-space and its basic formula
rubrics_metrics.description: Define P_t(x) = c_N t / ( (t^2 + |x|^2)^{(N+1)/2} ) for t>0 with explicit constant c_N (Lemma 8.17 / definition). This is the Poisson kernel for R^{N}_+.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lemma 8.17 computes the inverse Fourier transform of e^{-2π t |y|} to obtain the explicit Pt formula. Use dilations and known 1D Fourier transforms of (1+v^2)^{-1} to derive the general RN formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Properties of the Poisson kernel and semigroup
rubrics_metrics.description: For fixed t>0, P_t is continuous, integrable with integral 1, positive, satisfies P_t * P_s = P_{t+s}, and P_t → δ (approximate identity) as t → 0 (Proposition 8.18). Also P(x,t) is harmonic in the half-space variables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These properties follow from the explicit formula and Fourier analysis. The semigroup property and normalization (integral 1) make Pt a mollifier giving harmonic extensions (Poisson integrals) and are essential for boundary-value analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poisson integral boundary convergence and maximal estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: Let u(x,t) = P_t * f be the Poisson integral of f. For p=1,2,∞: (b) u(·,t) → f in L^p as t↓0 (for p<∞) under stated hypotheses; (c) uniform convergence on points of continuity when f∈L∞ and uniformly continuous on E; (e) a maximal inequality: measure{x: sup_{t>0} |P_t * f(x)| > ξ} ≤ C ||f||_1/ξ; (f) Fatou: u(x,t) → f(x) for a.e. x. (Theorem 8.19, parts (a)-(f)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The theorem spells out the senses in which the Poisson integral recovers boundary data: harmonicity, L^p convergence, uniform convergence at continuity points, weak-type (1,1) maximal control, and almost-everywhere pointwise convergence. Proofs use Fourier transform, maximal function theorems, density arguments (L^2 dense subspaces), and Poisson kernel estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic multiplier for harmonic extension
rubrics_metrics.description: When seeking a bounded operator that maps f(x) to u(x,t) harmonic in x with boundary f, the Fourier-side multiplier is m_t(y) = e^{-2π t |y|}; that is u(·,t) = F^{-1}( e^{-2π t |·|} · F f ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derivation: impose semigroup property m_{t+t1} = m_t m_{t1} and harmonicity (Laplace equation), leading to m_t(y)=e^{t g(y)} and deduce g(y) = -2π |y| from the PDE. Validated by computing inverse Fourier transform to obtain Poisson kernel Pt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conjugate Poisson kernel and Cauchy–Riemann relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Define Q_ε(x) (conjugate Poisson kernel) and its relation Q_ε * f = v(x,ε) (conjugate Poisson integral). Pair (u,v) = (P_ε * f, Q_ε * f) satisfies the Cauchy–Riemann equations and v is harmonic (Proposition 8.21). The L^2 Fourier transform of Q_ε equals i (sgn y) e^{-2πε|y|}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Q_ε is not L1 but belongs to L2; convolution Q_ε * f is defined for f∈L2. These conjugate kernels are the bridge between harmonic conjugates and Fourier multiplier i sgn; they are used to construct the Hilbert transform as a limit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hilbert transform as Fourier multiplier and principal value integral
rubrics_metrics.description: On L2(R1), the Hilbert transform H is given by the Fourier multiplier Ĥ f (y) = - i (sgn y) F f(y). Equivalently, Hf is the L2-limit as ε→0 of convolution with h_ε where h(x)=1/(π x): Hf(x) = lim_{ε→0} (1/π) ∫_{|t|>ε} f(x-t)/t dt in L2 (Theorems 8.22 and 8.24).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct H as limit of conjugate Poisson integrals Q_ε*f and use Plancherel and density to pass limits in L2. Also decompose kernels into Q_ε and a compactly supported part √_ε to manage convergence. The principal-value integral representation follows from this approximation procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boundedness/extension remarks for Hilbert transform
rubrics_metrics.description: H is a bounded linear operator on L2 and extends (with further work in next chapter) to a bounded operator on L^p(R1) for 1<p<∞. H does not extend to a bounded operator on L1: the Fourier multiplier i sgn(y) need not be the Fourier transform of an L1 function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The failure at p=1 is indicated by continuity considerations of transforms; boundedness on L^p (1<p<∞) will be established later. Use L2 Plancherel arguments for the initial construction and then interpolation/Calderón–Zygmund techniques for L^p bounds.
